content: Instead of checking that this command has been run (effectively) in CI, why don't we just run it?
Is it a file permission for CI issue?

And then have the workflow commit this change to the branch? You could do this, yes. Originally for instance we had lint-style-action configured with the option for a bot to act similarly. I changed this because I was frustrated by the unreliability of the action (reviewdog) this relied on, which would let lints silent pass undetected. I'd definitely consider a PR for mk_all that didn't have these issues.

CI steps that push changes to branches can often be confusing when working with git, as they leave the user out of sync with the remote. This can be risky, because if users learn "you can just force push because the change was just a bot on the remote", you now have users who are trained to force-push over any manually-authored modifications from maintainers.

Yeah, I personally prefer the simplicity of just having CI be simple checks with an exit code. Especially with the workflow on PRs also being used for the merge queue checks, I don't think it's worth the potential confusion and CI complexity for something that is trivial to fix yourself.

The potential of pre-commit is worth the confusion IMO. Automatically fixing all whitespace issues and in the future maybe running Skimmer sounds great.
Also, for git noobs using VSCode it's easier to click the "pull and then push" button which takes care of this automatically (assuming no conflicts), that button is right next to the commit button. The "just push" button is harder to find (it's hidden inside a hamburger menu, or in the "graph" view below).
The only way they can learn to force-push is if ChatGPT tells them to do so in a terminal.

Re: Skimmer, I was thinking of us starting with a similar setup to #36712. The first use case I was going to try out was semiautomating the mergeWithGrind weekly linting, but this still requires human intervention for a variety of reasons.
